Government involvement/regulations is why the problem exists in pharmacy with the poor reimbursements from PBM's. They are working within the constraints and rules written by the government.

More government involvement won't solve the problem and I don't have much faith in any government involvement saving this profession. 

When I was in college over 30 years ago we were discussing pharmacist's getting paid for their professional expertise with medication therapy management. 

Here we are over 30 years later and it's still being slow rolled out with very little change. 

80% of the total medication costs in the US is attributed to just 20% of the medications available. They are for chronic conditions such as diabetes, COPD, hypertension etc in mostly older adults. 

A small percentage of these people will have poor outcomes with their medication therapies and end up reentering the health care system for additional medical care. It can be right diagnosis, right therapy but something else contributes to the failed treatment. This is where pharmacy can make impact on real costs of healthcare...getting paid for our time and expertise to improve medication outcomes with coordination with our patient's other providers of care.

The PBM Act (S.1967) would delink PBM revenue from drug list prices in Medicare, banning spread pricing and requiring transparent reporting of rebates retained from manufacturers. This aligns with CMS efforts to ensure pharmacy reimbursements reflect actual drug costs rather than post-sale clawbacks. 

PBMs exploit offshore Group Purchasing Organizations (GPOs) in Ireland/Switzerland to avoid U.S. oversight while colluding to inflate generic drug markups. They steer patients to affiliated pharmacies through opaque reimbursement schemes—a practice the House Oversight Committee identified as systematically undermining independent pharmacies. Final reforms must uproot structural conflicts: Ban PBMs from owning pharmacies, end formulary manipulation by excluding PBM-affiliated entities from Medicare Part D’s Pharmacy & Therapeutics committees, and mandate real-time disclosure of off-formulary drug pricing disparities to expose therapeutic equivalence markups. 

The path forward requires overriding health insurer lobbying to implement these measures—without half-measures that let PBMs rebuild profit channels through offshore entities or specialty drug steering.
